articles.title: France's Competition Chief Puts SFR Deal on Notice
articles.subtitle: Benoît Coeuré warned the €20.35B three-way acquisition 'does not go without saying,' citing a 2005 price-collusion precedent from France's last three-operator market.
articles.body_md:
The French competition regulator delivered the SFR deal's first institutional setback four days after the June 6 binding MOU was signed. **Benoît Coeuré**, president of the **Autorité de la concurrence** (AdC), told Le Monde on June 10 that the **€20.35B** three-way SFR acquisition "ne va pas de soi" — does not go without saying. That phrasing, from a sitting competition authority president rather than an operator's public relations desk, is a substantively different signal from the behavioral-remedies framing **Orange** CEO Anne Heydemann offered before the ink was dry on June 6.

## Why the 2005 Precedent Changes the Risk Profile

Coeuré's specific reference to the 2005 price-collusion case carries analytical weight. France's mobile market ran as a three-operator structure under **Orange**, **SFR**, and **Bouygues** through the early 2000s. All three were ultimately fined for illegal coordination on retail prices. The SFR deal would recreate precisely that structure. For AdC, the collusion history is not mere context — it is documented evidence that three-player French mobile markets carry coordination risk that a behavioral remedy package may not adequately address.

## Parallel Regulatory Tracks Complicate the Timeline

The jurisdictional structure adds procedural weight. **Bouygues** and **Orange**, whose revenues are predominantly French, will file notifications with AdC. **Free (Iliad)**, whose international revenue weight triggers mandatory EC filing, must file separately with the **European Commission** — creating parallel tracks that could generate conflicting signals or rival remedy frameworks. The EC could assert sole jurisdiction and remove AdC entirely; alternatively, both regulators could run simultaneous reviews with no guarantee of coordinated outcomes.

No formal pre-notification has been received by AdC as of June 10. Definitive documents are expected H2 2026; the AdC process runs approximately **18 months** from formal filing, implying regulatory close no earlier than **H2 2027**. At that timeline, the break-up fees — ranging from **€100M to €2B** — provide exit optionality but do not resolve the regulators' substantive concerns.

## What to Watch

First formal pre-notification filings (H2 2026) and whether the EC asserts sole jurisdiction; pre-notification dialogue — any hint of structural remedy pre-proposals (spectrum or infrastructure divestiture) from the three buyers; the AdC's referral decision and timing; Romania's post-merger consumer price data as empirical counter-evidence to the French price-risk thesis.
articles.summary: French competition authority president Benoît Coeuré warned on June 10 that the €20.35B SFR three-way deal 'does not go without saying,' citing a 2005 price-collusion case from France's last three-operator market. Parallel regulatory filings (AdC and EC), no formal notification yet, and break-up fees of €100M–€2B make H2 2027 closing contingent on structural remedy negotiations.

articles.title: FCC Closes the Last Security Gap in US Submarine Cable Infrastructure
articles.subtitle: The June 25 SLTE order bars Chinese-linked entities from end-terminal hardware at US cable-landing points, completing a three-layer governance architecture alongside EU and GUIDE frameworks.
articles.body_md:
Previously, a Chinese entity could be legally barred from owning a submarine cable system while still supplying the **Submarine Line Terminal Equipment** — the hardware at the cable head that converts optical signals into terrestrial network traffic. The **FCC**'s Second Report and Order, published June 4 and scheduled for a June 25 vote, closes that gap.

The mechanism is a blanket licence framework for non-disqualified SLTE owners and operators, paired with a mandatory annual reporting requirement for any entity on the **FCC Covered List** (which includes **Huawei**, **ZTE**, and their affiliates) or subject to a foreign adversary designation. In practice, **HMN Technologies** — formerly Huawei Marine Networks, the world's largest submarine cable system manufacturer — cannot own or operate SLTE equipment at any US-landing cable point. The parallels to the German 5G core exclusion are direct: the same Covered List mechanism applied to a different layer of the same strategic infrastructure.

## Compliance Implications for European Operators

For European cable consortia with US-landing segments, the order introduces a vendor audit requirement that is new but structurally familiar. Any cable landing in the US must now verify its SLTE vendor against the Covered List annually. **Nokia Submarine Networks**, **Subcom (TE SubCom)**, and **Alcatel Submarine Networks** — the three non-Covered-List Tier 1 cable system suppliers — are the clear beneficiaries of Chinese exclusion, both in new-build procurements and in potential SLTE retrofit requirements on existing systems.

## Three Governance Layers Around the Same Infrastructure

The FCC order is the third framework established around submarine cable infrastructure in under three weeks. The EU's **Cable Security Toolbox** (released early June 2026) addresses civilian governance and critical infrastructure resilience. **GUIDE** (launched May 30, 2026) provides military and intelligence information sharing across **17 nations**, including 7 EU member states and the UK. The FCC order addresses the equipment layer. No single framework spans the full governance stack, but the combined architecture is the most comprehensive multilateral structure for submarine cable security ever assembled.

## What to Watch

The June 25 FCC vote outcome and any commissioner dissent on trade policy grounds; European cable consortium SLTE vendor transition timelines; whether the EU Cable Security Toolbox adopts an equivalent SLTE-level equipment standard; GUIDE operational protocols for intelligence sharing on Covered List entities operating near cable infrastructure.
articles.summary: The FCC's Second Submarine Cable R&O, due for a June 25 vote, extends US regulatory authority to terminal hardware at cable-landing points — barring Chinese-linked entities from SLTE ownership and requiring Covered List entities to file annual compliance reports. The order completes a three-layer governance architecture alongside the EU's Cable Security Toolbox and the 17-nation GUIDE framework.

articles.title: atNorth's 350MW Norway Campus Locks In Europe's Power Arbitrage Leader
articles.subtitle: CPP Investments and Equinix back a $1.1B Phase 1 at Haugaland with Statnett grid infrastructure — bringing Norway's total announced AI hyperscale pipeline to ~580MW.
articles.body_md:
**Norway** now has two large-scale AI compute campuses in active development. **atNorth**'s June 3 announcement of NOR01 at Haugaland Business Park adds **350MW** (full build) and **NOK 11B** (~$1.1B) in Phase 1 investment to the **230MW** Nscale Narvik campus (Edition 13), bringing Norway's total announced AI hyperscale pipeline to approximately **580MW**. That is more committed capacity than the Netherlands — the third-ranked FLAP-D market — added in the prior 18 months, at roughly one-seventh the power cost.

## Ownership Structure as Strategic Signal

**CPP Investments** (60%, ~$1.6B) and **Equinix** (40%) acquired atNorth from **Partners Group** for **$4B** enterprise value in February 2026. Equinix is deploying its first Norwegian colocation footprint through NOR01, giving hyperscaler customers direct interconnection access at the campus. For AI compute workloads, removing the network hop between a compute campus and the broader interconnection fabric is material — the latency premium of third-party routing to an Equinix PoP typically ranges 3–8ms for European enterprise endpoints. NOR01 eliminates that premium for colocation customers.

## Grid Commitment Confirms National Industrial Status

**Statnett**, Norway's transmission system operator, is building a dedicated substation for NOR01 alongside a second substation from regional operator **Fagne**. TSO-dedicated grid infrastructure for a private data centre campus is the same model used at Nscale Narvik, where **Eksfin** — Norway's export credit agency — co-funded the $790M infrastructure debt facility. When a national TSO builds dedicated infrastructure for a private campus, it signals classification as national industrial infrastructure — carrying the queue priority and capex commitment that most European markets are still debating as policy proposals.

Norway's power pricing at the Haugesund node remains approximately **€0.04/kWh**, maintaining roughly a 7x advantage over UK industrial electricity at **24.67p/kWh** (~€0.30/kWh) and a 5x advantage over FLAP-D prime market averages. atNorth's broader pipeline — **800MW** installed or active plus **1GW+** of secured power for future expansion — positions the platform to extend this advantage into Finland and Sweden as hyperscaler demand for energy-advantaged AI compute continues to grow.

## What to Watch

First hyperscaler customer announcement for NOR01 (likely H2 2026 to anchor the 2028 power target); Statnett substation construction timeline; atNorth's next campus location (the 1GW+ secured pipeline remains undeployed); total CPP Investments European DC allocation crossing $5B as the Goodman FLAP-D JV enters construction simultaneously.
articles.summary: atNorth's 350MW Haugaland campus ($1.1B Phase 1) brings Norway's total announced AI hyperscale pipeline to ~580MW alongside Nscale Narvik. CPP Investments and Equinix back the platform via a $4B acquisition, while Statnett's dedicated substation confirms Norway's grid-priority classification — maintaining a ~7x power cost advantage over UK industrial electricity.

articles.title: Goodman and CPP Break Ground on 435MW European Data Centre Platform
articles.subtitle: Four FLAP-D projects enter construction by June 30 with power and permits already secured — separating this platform from the majority of Europe's grid-queued pipeline.
articles.body_md:
**Goodman Group** and **CPP Investments** commence construction across all four projects in their **European Data Centre Partnership** by **June 30, 2026** — delivering **435MW** of primary power capacity and **282MW** of hyperscaler-lease-ready IT load across Paris (two sites), Frankfurt, and Amsterdam. All four sites enter construction with power connections, planning permits, and substantially completed site infrastructure already secured. That qualifier separates the platform from the majority of European greenfield data centre pipelines, which remain in grid intake freezes in the UK (~125 GW queue, ~140 data centres waiting), Ireland (CRU generation obligation restructuring connection costs), and the Netherlands (Amsterdam grid moratorium).

## JV Structure and Capital Profile

The joint venture was announced in December 2025 at an **€8B** (A$14B) total platform capacity, with an initial commitment of **€2.2B** (A$3.9B) at a 50/50 split. **Goodman Group** contributes European industrial real estate development capability — the group runs one of the continent's largest logistics portfolios — combined with existing site and planning relationships in all three target markets. **CPP Investments** contributes long-duration infrastructure capital from a pension mandate with a multi-decade investment horizon. The develop-to-own model Goodman employs in logistics maps directly: anchor hyperscaler pre-leases at contracted returns, institutional balance sheet holding the asset, long-term income generation.

## FLAP-D Concentration is Deliberate

Paris, Frankfurt, and Amsterdam remain the three highest-liquidity hyperscaler interconnection markets in Europe. Concentrating initial build in markets where grid access is already secured minimises the primary execution risk — grid delay — that has pushed European greenfield timelines from 18 to 36+ months for sites without pre-secured connections. The **282MW** of IT-load-ready capacity across the four projects aligns with the anchor customer pre-lease format used by **Google**, **Microsoft**, **Meta**, and **Amazon** in their FLAP-D RFP processes.

## CPP's Bifurcated European Strategy

CPP Investments' portfolio now spans both sides of Europe's DC investment bifurcation: **FLAP-D prime colocation** (Goodman JV, 50%, entering construction) and **Nordic AI compute edge** (**atNorth**, 60%, NOR01 announced June 3 at 350MW). With total European DC allocation approaching **$5B**, CPP is among the largest single institutional holders of European DC capacity across geographies — a positioning that few pension funds globally have replicated.

## What to Watch

First hyperscaler pre-lease announcements for PAR01, PAR02, FRA02, AMS01 (expected H2 2026–H1 2027); whether Goodman extends into non-FLAP markets (Italy, Spain, Poland — the HSCALE thesis); CPP total European DC allocation crossing $10B; Goodman DC revenue as a percentage of group full-year 2026 results.
articles.summary: Goodman Group and CPP Investments begin construction by June 30 on four European DC sites (Paris ×2, Frankfurt, Amsterdam) delivering 435MW with power and planning pre-secured. CPP now holds ~$5B of European DC exposure across FLAP-D (Goodman JV) and Nordic AI compute (atNorth), representing one of the largest bifurcated European DC allocations among pension funds globally.

articles.title: Romania Becomes the EU's Second 4→3 Mobile Market in Three Months
articles.subtitle: OTE's €70M distressed exit and Digi's spectrum gain at €40M set the structural remedy template France's competition regulator will apply to the €20.35B SFR review.
articles.body_md:
**Romania** formally became a three-operator mobile market on **June 30, 2026**, when **Vodafone Romania** and **Telekom Romania Mobile Communications** completed their legal merger. The headline deal value is instructive: **OTE** — the **Deutsche Telekom** subsidiary and Telekom Romania parent — sold a national mobile operator for a combined **€70M**, implying enterprise value near zero for network infrastructure that would cost hundreds of millions to rebuild from greenfield.

## Asset Split Reveals Accepted Remedy Architecture

The division between two acquirers reveals the remedy structure regulators accepted. **Vodafone** paid **€30M** for the postpaid customer book, retail store network, and technical network infrastructure — the B2B and enterprise-grade assets that strengthen its competitive position against market leader **Orange Romania**. **Digi** paid **€40M** for the prepaid customer base, spectrum licences, and tower assets. Those spectrum rights would command **€200M+** in a competitive auction. Digi's acquisition at €40M is a regulator-enabled subsidy to the market's emerging challenger — the argument that a three-player market can retain a credible competitive threat if the smallest player holds adequate spectrum capacity.

## The EU's Consolidation Template is Now Empirical

This is the **second EU 4→3 mobile consolidation** in 2026, following the UK's **VodafoneThree** closure in April. Two markets in one quarter, under a regulatory posture shaped by the Draghi Report's emphasis on investment capacity over operator count. The EU consolidation thesis has moved from hypothetical to empirical, and the debate now shifts to consumer outcomes.

Romania is a cost-sensitive market with high prepaid penetration and structurally elevated churn. If average revenue per user rises materially within 12–18 months of the merger, the consolidation-causes-price-increases thesis gains its first EU empirical validation. If ARPU holds or falls, it weakens the primary argument **Benoît Coeuré** at the **Autorité de la concurrence** is building in the **SFR** review — that three-player markets reliably produce higher consumer prices.

## What to Watch

Romania consumer price and ARPU data 12–18 months post-merger — the direct empirical test for the SFR regulatory debate; Digi Romania spectrum deployment and network quality trajectory; OTE's repatriation of €70M proceeds to Greek capex; whether the AdC cites Romania as a precedent in SFR pre-notification dialogue.
articles.summary: Romania's June 30 legal merger between Vodafone and Telekom Romania completes the EU's second 4→3 mobile consolidation in three months, with OTE exiting at a €70M combined price — near-zero enterprise value. Digi's spectrum acquisition at €40M establishes the structural remedy template that the Autorité de la concurrence will evaluate in the €20.35B SFR process.
